niche.title: The Circle of Willis Trap Most Students Fall For
niche.description:
Everyone learns the big vessels of the circle of Willis. Almost nobody remembers what closes the ring.

At the front the internal carotids give off the anterior and middle cerebral arteries. At the back the vertebrals unite as the basilar, which gives off the posterior cerebrals. Three communicating arteries close the circle: one anterior and two posterior. And the posterior cerebral arteries typically arise from the basilar, not the carotids.

📚 Get the circle of Willis in full, with labelled illustrations, a video on the brain arteries and quizzes covering every vessel: https://khub.me/dsfl8

niche.title: 8 Cranial Bones Mnemonic: Old People From Texas Eat Spiders | Skull Anatomy #shorts
niche.description:
Can you name all 8 cranial bones? One silly sentence does it: Old People From Texas Eat Spiders 🦴

O → Occipital: the back of your skull (the spinal cord exits through its foramen magnum)
P → Parietal: top and sides (a pair)
F → Frontal: your forehead
T → Temporal: right above your ears (a pair)
E → Ethmoid: tucked between your eye sockets
S → Sphenoid: the "keystone" that joins almost every other skull bone
6 names, but parietal and temporal come in pairs = 8 cranial bones.

Quick test: your spinal cord leaves the skull through which bone? Answer in the video.

niche.title: When You Lose Fat, You Breathe Most of It Out
niche.description:
Lose ten pounds of fat, and where does it actually go? Mostly into the air you breathe out.

Fat is made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, so once your body has used it, what's left is carbon dioxide and water. By the numbers, about 8.4 of those ten pounds leave your lungs as carbon dioxide, and the other 1.6 leave as water in urine, sweat and other fluids (a calculation published in the BMJ in 2014).

Breathing faster won't speed it up, though. Your body has to use the fat first.

This is general health information, not medical advice.

niche.title: Where does your snot go if you don't blow?
niche.description:
You swallow it. All day, without noticing.
Glands in your nose and throat make mucus all the time. It traps dust and germs from the air you breathe in, then slides to the back of your throat, mixes with saliva, and you swallow it down your food pipe. Your lungs' airways make mucus too, and tiny hairs called cilia lift it up toward your throat, where it is swallowed or coughed out.
You mostly notice mucus when there is extra, like with a cold or cold air.

🏥 Commonly performed during:
🔹 General anesthesia
🔹 Respiratory failure
🔹 Severe emergencies
🔹 Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)
